summaries.example: Imagine two groups performing the same dance. The first group follows a written plan, but the dancers add small movements of their own. The second group changes the dance each time. Are both performances the same dance? Philosophers ask whether a dance is mainly a plan, a repeatable pattern, a live event, or something that grows through practice.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of dance explores questions about dancing as art and as human activity. One question is definitional: what separates dance from other kinds of movement? Another is about identity: what makes a dance the same dance when different people perform it at different times? Some thinkers focus on choreography, scores, or repeatable patterns. Others focus on the dancers’ bodies, choices, feelings, and live experiences. Dance is often called ephemeral because it changes and vanishes while it happens. Philosophers disagree about whether this makes dance difficult to preserve or gives live dance a special power. They also study improvisation, audience bodily responses, cultural practices, technology, and the role of real dance-world knowledge. There is no single agreed answer, so philosophy of dance uses several approaches.
key_ideas: Philosophers ask what makes a movement dance rather than ordinary movement.
They disagree about whether a dance is a pattern, a performance, an event, or a process.
A dance may be changed, revived, reconstructed, or reenacted, and these activities are not always the same.
Dance is bodily and temporary, but its temporary nature may be a problem or a valuable part of its beauty.
Dancers, choreographers, audiences, and communities can all matter when we decide what a dance is.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dance is more than moving to music. It can be art, a social activity, a way to learn, and a way people express themselves. Thinking about dance helps us notice the work of dancers and choreographers, understand why live performances feel special, and ask how old dances can be remembered or changed. It also reminds us that different communities and kinds of dancing may require different ways of thinking.

important_terms.definition: Thinking carefully about what dance is, how it works, and why it matters.
A dance that changes or disappears as it is performed instead of remaining as a permanent object.
A dance made to be performed more than once, even when each performance is a little different.
The power to make choices and guide one’s own actions while dancing.

questions_to_think_about: If a dancer changes an important movement, is it still the same dance?
Can a video or written plan save a dance completely?
Why might someone enjoy a live dance more than a recording?
When dancers improvise, how much freedom do they really have?

summaries.example: Suppose a choreographer gives dancers a score with a sequence and timing, but leaves some gestures open. Years later, another group studies the score, interviews people who saw the first performance, and creates a new version. One philosopher might say the score identifies a repeatable work. Another might treat the work as an action-structure shaped by historical and artistic practices. A third might emphasize the performance event and the dancers’ embodied contributions. The disagreement concerns ontology—what kind of thing a dance artwork is—and identity—what makes it the same work across performances.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of dance is a broad and interdisciplinary field concerned with dance as art, embodied activity, social practice, and technologically mediated performance. In analytic aesthetics, three recurring problems are definition, ontology, and identity. Philosophers ask what distinguishes dance from other movement, what sort of thing a dance artwork is, and how one work can remain the same across performances. Proposed answers treat works as score-based structures, types instantiated in performances, action-structures, or entities whose identity depends on choreographic purposes and danceworld practices. Other approaches give priority to the felt and bodily character of performance rather than to an underlying object or score. Dance’s ephemerality intensifies these issues: its movements disappear as they occur, yet that impermanence may either threaten preservation or help make live dance aesthetically powerful. The field also examines re-performance, revival, reconstruction, reenactment, improvisation, authorship, agency, kinaesthetic audience responses, and the use of cognitive science. Methodological disagreements concern how much weight to give practice, lived experience, community knowledge, and empirical research. The entry also points toward philosophical work on non-Western and vernacular traditions, ethics and politics, disability, film, digital technology, and artificial intelligence.
key_ideas: Analytic aesthetics often organizes dance philosophy around definition, ontology, and identity, but some philosophers resist the search for a single essential definition of dance.
Accounts of dance ontology include scores, recipes, types, action-types, community-based purposes, and appreciative practices; these approaches prioritize different features of dance art.

Because notation, recordings, memories, and later performances can diverge, re-performance, revival, reconstruction, and reenactment raise distinct questions about preservation and historical knowledge.
Ephemerality can be understood negatively, as a threat to repeatability and survival, or positively, as a source of the live performance’s intensity and uniqueness.

Dance involves intentional and embodied action. Agency may belong to individual dancers, choreographers, audiences, or temporary groups, and performers may be interpreters, creators, coauthors, or some combination depending on the theory.

Philosophers disagree about kinaesthetic responses and scientific evidence: some see bodily responses and cognitive science as relevant to appreciation, while others limit or reject their philosophical importance.
summaries.why_it_matters: Philosophy of dance tests theories of art against an art form that is embodied, temporal, collaborative, and difficult to capture fully in words or notation. It therefore illuminates broader questions about artistic identity, authorship, interpretation, memory, expertise, and the relation between mind and body. Its disagreements also matter practically: how we preserve historical dances, evaluate performances, credit creative labor, understand audience experience, and decide whether screen-based or digitally produced movement gives us access to a dance artwork itself.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical question of what kind of entity a dance artwork is, such as an object, event, process, or repeatable structure.
The question of what makes one dance artwork numerically the same work through different performances and historical changes.
The view that a dance artwork can have multiple correct performances, even if those performances differ in some qualities.
The temporary, changing character of dance, especially the fact that live movement vanishes as it occurs.
Intentional, skilled action by dancers, choreographers, audiences, or groups; theories distinguish simple action, decision-making freedom, and shared or conflicted control.
A bodily response to perceived movement, sometimes involving tension, rhythm, excitement, or an imagined feeling of moving with the dancer.
Spontaneous or partly spontaneous movement within, between, or instead of fixed choreography.
A philosophical approach that treats bodily awareness and felt experience as important for understanding art and human activity.

questions_to_think_about: Should a philosophical account begin with actual dance practices, or may it revise dancers’ and audiences’ ordinary beliefs?
What features must remain stable for two performances to count as instances of one dance artwork?
Does a score preserve a dance, or can it become a starting point for a new work?
Are dancers merely interpreting choreography, or can their performance contributions make them artistic coauthors?
Can scientific explanations of bodily responses tell us what counts as proper artistic appreciation?

summaries.example: A school dance club learns a routine from an old video. The club keeps the main sequence but changes the speed, adds gestures, and lets each dancer respond to the others. One student says it is the original dance because the main pattern remains. Another says it is a new performance because the dancers’ choices change the work. A third says the video shows only one past event, not the dance itself. Philosophers use cases like this to explore identity, authorship, preservation, and improvisation.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of dance asks how to understand dancing as art, action, bodily experience, and cultural practice. A central debate begins with three questions: how to distinguish dance from other movement, what kind of thing a dance artwork is, and how a work stays the same through repeated performances. Some philosophers favor structures recorded in scores or described by a recipe. Others treat dance artworks as repeatable action-types shaped by historical circumstances, artistic purposes, and the norms of dance communities. Still others think the most important features are the performers’ bodies, sensations, choices, and the audience’s experience. Dance is often described as ephemeral because its movement is fleeting and continually changing. This can make preservation and identity difficult, but it can also explain the special force of being present at a live event. The field studies different forms of returning to older dances, the creative roles of choreographers and dancers, improvisation, and agency. It also asks whether audience members’ bodily reactions provide knowledge about dance and whether cognitive science can help explain those reactions. The broader field includes many cultural traditions, social dances, ethical and political questions, and dance made for film or digital technologies.
key_ideas: Philosophers ask three connected questions: what counts as dance, what sort of thing a dance artwork is, and what makes it the same work over time.
Some theories emphasize scores, choreographic structures, or repeatable patterns. Other theories emphasize live bodies, artistic communities, and changing practice.
Dance notation and recordings can help preserve dance, but they may not determine every detail of later performances.
Re-performing, reviving, reconstructing, and reenacting a dance are different ways of returning to the past, though their boundaries can be unclear.
Improvisation can mean adding flourishes, filling a planned gap, or creating much of the performance while dancing. Claims about freedom must consider social and physical limits.
Audience members may experience bodily reactions while watching dance. Philosophers disagree about whether these reactions help us identify artistic qualities or are only personal responses.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates show why dance cannot be understood only as a sequence of physical motions. They help us think about how art is made, repeated, remembered, and experienced. They also make room for the knowledge of dancers, choreographers, audiences, and communities, while showing that no single method—written analysis, bodily experience, scientific research, or practice alone—settles every philosophical question about dance.

important_terms.definition: The study of what dance is, what dance artworks are, and why dancing is important to human life.
A philosophical account of what kind of thing a dance artwork is: for example, a pattern, event, process, or something repeatable.
The problem of explaining how a dance can remain the same artwork when it is performed by different dancers at different times.
A quality of live dance in which movement changes and passes away as it happens; it does not mean that dance is unimportant.
The ability of a dancer or group to act intentionally and make choices, including cases where control is shared or partly limited.
Movement created spontaneously, either as an addition to choreography, in an open section, or throughout a performance.
A bodily sense or response connected with movement, such as feeling tension, rhythm, excitement, or an imagined motion while watching.

questions_to_think_about: What should matter most when deciding whether two performances are the same dance?
Could a dance survive without a written score or continuous performances?
When does a dancer’s contribution become creation rather than interpretation?
Does improvisation make a performance freer, or does it simply replace one set of rules with another?
Why might a live performance give an experience that a video cannot fully reproduce?
